2.text: Stories about such beings form the greater part of the folk-lore and

3.text: mythology of the Chukchee. Most prominent among them are the keˊlet

4.text: (pl. of keˊlᴇ). Of these there are several classes, all of which may do harm

5.text: to mankind. Sometimes, however, all kinds of spirits, harmful or harmless,

6.text: are referred to as keˊlet; but, strictly speaking, this use of the term is incor-

7.text: rect. An accurate speaker will distinguish at least two separate classes of

8.text: supernatural beings, — the harmful keˊlᴇ or evil spirit and the benevolent

10.text: Many times when witnessing sacrifices made by the common people,

11.text: who know little of spiritual matters, I asked to whom the sacrifice was being

12.text: proffered. The answer was, “Who knows! To the vaˊɪrg̣ɪn, to the keˊlᴇ

13.text: (“Qo! vaɪrg̣êˊtɪ, kalag̣tɪˊ”). Both names were intended for the class of beings

14.text: friendly to man, because no Chukchee will openly confess to having made

15.text: sacrifices to evil spirits, except under extraordinary circumstances.

16.text: The word “vaˊɪrg̣ɪn” (pl. vaˊɪrg̣ɪt) signifies simply “being,” and therefore

17.text: keˊlet may also be called by this name. In this case some additional identi-

18.text: fication is usually desired. For example, aqaˊm-vaˊɪrg̣ɪt indicates “bad

21.text: I mentioned also that the “owners” of the rivers, lakes, etc., are also

22.text: called keˊlet. This is analogous to the fact that nymphs, dryads, and other

23.text: genii of the Greeks and Romans, were also called gods, and were supposed

24.text: to have various relations with higher deities, even to have sexual intercourse

25.text: with them. All three classes of supernatural beings are also called by the

26.text: Chukchee “the clever ones” (g̣ɪtteˊpɪčɪt), as people versed in magic are called

28.text: COMPARATIVE NOTES. — Judging from my own information and that

29.text: collected by Mr. Jochelson, the religious ideas of the Koryak present many

30.text: close similarities to those of the Chukchee, not only in their general character,

31.text: but also in their way of development. Thus, Mr. Jochelson says that

32.text: “household utensils, implements, parts of the house, the chamber-vessel, and

33.text: even excrement, have an existence of their own. They may warn their

34.text: ‘masters’ of danger, and attack their enemies.”¹ This corresponds to what

35.text: I call the “first stage of development.” Mr. Jochelson also mentions that

36.text: the “anthropomorphic ideas of the Koryak are schematic and incomplete,”

37.text: though, “on the other hand, the vagueness of their notions does not prevent

38.text: them from being material.”² He points out this vagueness in regard par-

39.text: ticularly to their wooden images of a religious kind, whose outlines are very

40.text: crude. I rank such vague attempts in the second stage and in the first step of

41.text: development of the anthropomorphic conception. Mr. Jochelson says, also, that
